title: Gary Morrow, cancer research pioneer, dies at 82 after long illness
text:
Gary Morrow, cancer research pioneer, dies at 82 after long illness
M. G. Ayers
Gary R. Morrow, PhD, MS, a leader at the University of Rochester Medicine Wilmot Cancer Institute and a pioneer in supportive care research for cancer patients, died on July 7 after complications from pneumonia. He was 82 and had lived with prostate cancer for 16 years.
Morrow was recognized for his commitment to improving quality of life for cancer patients by addressing symptoms such as nausea and side effects from treatment. His work contributed to the development of anti-emetic drugs that control chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting—considered one of the top five advances in cancer care over the past half-century by the American Society of Clinical Oncology.
Hucky Land, PhD, Wilmot deputy director, said: “Facing up to the fact that medicine doesn’t have all the answers and turning that into an opportunity was very important. Gary has done that against all odds. It is a very rare achievement.”
During nearly five decades at the University of Rochester, Morrow secured $100 million in funding and mentored many future leaders in supportive oncology care. Jonathan W. Friedberg, MD, MMSc, said: “Gary’s commitment to supporting the next generation of investigators...has resulted in an outstanding legacy.” Colleagues described him as demanding but dedicated to patient-centered care before it became standard practice.
Morrow applied clinical psychology principles to oncology when few considered patient experiences during treatment. George Abraham, MD, said: “He persisted through times when people did not appreciate what patients were going through...He had the innate sense that if you can ameliorate side effects you can improve therapy.”
His research defined anticipatory nausea as a barrier to completing treatment and led high-profile studies published in major journals like NEJM and JAMA. In 1999 he served on an expert panel establishing national guidelines for anti-nausea medication use during chemotherapy.
Lori Minasian, MD, said: “His passion for research extended into training and he led an NCI-sponsored cancer symptom management training program for over 30 years...His legacy will live on through the many investigators that he trained.”
Morrow also founded influential programs including Wilmot’s Cancer Control group—continuously funded by NCI—and helped establish community-based clinical trials networks now known as NCORP.
Calling hours are scheduled for Thursday, July 23 from 4 p.m.–7 p.m., with funeral services Friday, July 24 at St. John’s Chapel in Geneva.
